terms.definition: The study of how history is researched, interpreted, and written.
Dividing history into named eras to make change over time easier to study.
Evidence created by people who lived during the period under study.
Testing a source by comparing it with independent evidence.
The conditions and ideas surrounding an event or source.
The movement of plants, animals, diseases, people, and ideas between hemispheres after 1492.
The authority of a people or government to govern itself.
Colonization aimed at permanent settlement and control of Indigenous land.
An economic policy linking colonies to the wealth and power of an imperial state.
Labor performed for a fixed term in exchange for passage, support, or debt repayment.
The belief that government should serve the public good through representatives and civic virtue.
Rights understood as inherent to human beings rather than granted by rulers.
The principle that legitimate government rests on the consent of the governed.
Collective refusal to buy goods or participate in activity as political pressure.
A colonist who remained loyal to Britain during the American Revolution.
A system dividing authority between national and state governments.
Division of governmental powers among branches.
Constitutional mechanisms allowing branches to restrain one another.
Formal approval of a constitution, treaty, or amendment.
The power of courts to assess whether government action is constitutional.
